Lost and found
The first thing Adrian noticed when he stepped off the bus was the silence. The town of
Sungai Merah had not changed much since he left ten years ago, yet it felt unfamiliar, as if time
had rearranged it without his permission. The old clock tower still stood at the centre of the town
but its paint was peeling, and the hands moved more slowly than he remembered. Adrian tightened
his grip on his bag and wondered whether returning had been a mistake.
He had left Sungai Merah in search of something better. Fresh out of school, he believed
that success could only be found elsewhere—in tall buildings, crowded streets and fast-paced lives.
The town had seemed too small for his ambitions, too quiet for his dreams. When he boarded the
bus that morning years ago, he promised himself that he would never look back. Yet here he was,
returning for his late grandmother's house, the last thing she had left behind.
The house stood at the end of a narrow lane, shaded by a mango tree that had grown taller
over the years. As Adrian pushed open the creaking gate, memories flooded his mind when he saw
the mango tree. He remembered sitting under it as a child, listening to his grandmother's stories
and believing that the world was full of possibilities. Those moments felt distant now, buried under
years of deadlines, disappointments and silent struggles. Adrian worked in a big corporate company
and had steadily climbed up the ranks. However, there were times when he wondered if it was all
worth it.
Inside the house, dust covered the furniture and the air smelled of age and neglect. Adrian
began sorting through old boxes, unsure of what he was searching for. Photographs, letters and
faded notebooks lay scattered across the floor. The next few boxes contained old clothes that he
decided to donate to charity. Then, in one corner, he found a small wooden box, beside a beautiful
ceramic vase, he had never seen before. Curious, he opened it and discovered a leather notebook,
its pages yellowed with time.
The notebook belonged to his grandmother. As Adrian flipped through the pages, he realised
it was a journal. As he read the journal line by line, page by page, the minutes turned into hours.
She had written about her hopes for her children and grandchildren, about her fears during difficult
times and about her belief that everyone would eventually find their way, no matter how far they
wandered. One sentence stood out to him: "Being lost is sometimes necessary, for it teaches us
what truly matters."
CS

Adrian closed the notebook and sat in silence. For years, he had measured success by
promotions and paychecks, yet he often felt empty. In chasing his dreams, he had lost touch with
his family, his values and even himself. The journal made him realise that what he had been
searching for was not a place but a sense of belonging.
Later that evening, Adrian walked through the town. He met familiar faces who greeted him
warmly, despite the years of absence. The local café owner remembered his favourite drink and an
old school friend invited him to catch up. With each conversation, Adrian felt a piece of himself
returning, as if the town was quietly giving back what he had once lost.
Before leaving, Adrian visited his grandmother's grave. He placed the notebook beside the
flowers and whispered a thank-you. He understood now that life was not just about moving forward
but also about knowing when to return. As the bus pulled away from the local bus station the next
morning, Adrian looked out at Sungai Merah with a sense of peace. He had come back to settle a
house, but he was leaving with something far more valuable—clarity, connection and the feeling
of being found.

Being a smart teenager
Being careful with money as a teenager does not mean one cannot spend on treats; it is
about being strategic. The financial habits you build now will determine whether you struggle or
thrive in your 20s. 27
First, treat your savings as a payment to yourself. This concept is
crucial. Do not wait to see what is left over at the end of the month because usually, nothing is
left. This means as soon as you receive money, immediately move 20-30% into a separate
savings account. 28
If you do not see the money in your checking account, you will not
be tempted to spend it.
Next, calculate the time cost. This concept is a game-changer. 29
For example, if
you earn RM 15 an hour and want a pair of RM 150 shoes, ask yourself: "Are these shoes worth
10 hours of my labour?" Often, we will tend to realise that the effort required to earn that money
makes the purchase feel unnecessary. 30
At the same time, you will save your money too.
Another aspect to take into consideration is your daily habits such as getting a drink at a
café, could drain your bank accounts faster than big purchases. An RM 5 coffee or energy drink
every day costs RM 150 a month! You do not have to cut everything out, but you must track it. (31) ______
You will probably surprise yourself when you notice how much you spend on something
as simple as a roti canai or nasi lemak! 32
Thrifting clothes or buying refurbished tech is
not only cheaper but often more sustainable. It is also a trend these days to create an awesome
ensemble of an outfit from clothes that are preloved. Be a smart teenager, you not only will look
great but also be saving more for your future.
